FOREWORD 


This Indian Standard was adopted by the Bureau of Indian Standards, after the draft finalized by the Clay and 
Stabilized Soil Products for Construction Sectional Committee had been approved by the Civil Engineering 
Division Council. 


Standard methods of testing burnt clay bricks are essential adjuncts to the various burnt clay brick specifications. 


This standard, IS 3495 was first published in 1966 and subsequently revised in 1973, 1976, 1992 and 2019 
covering four parts (Part | to Part 4). Earlier all the tests to evaluate the physical properties of burnt clay bricks 
were covered in one standard but for facilitating the use of this standard and future revisions, the revised standard 
was brought out in different parts, each part covering different test. 


This standard (Part 5) is a new addition to this series of standards and it explains the method of determination of 
initial rate of absorption of moisture in burnt clay bricks. This is a laboratory method. The other parts in this series 
now, are: 


Part 1 Determination of compressive strength 
Part 2 Determination of water absorption 
Part 3 Determination of efflorescence 
Part 4 Determination of warpage 
Part 6 Determination of modulus of rupture 
The composition of the Committee responsible for the formulation of this standard is given in Annex A. 


In reporting the result of a test or analysis made in accordance with this standard, if the final value observed or 
calculated, is to be rounded off, it shall be done in accordance with IS 2 : 1960 ‘Rules for rounding off numerical 
values ( revised )’. 


IS 3495 (Part 5) : 2021 


Indian Standard 


BURNT CLAY BUILDING 
BRICKS — METHODS OF TEST 


PART 5 DETERMINATION OF INITIAL RATE OF ABSORPTION 


1 SCOPE 


This standard (Part 5) covers the method of 
determination of initial rate of absorption in burnt clay 
bricks. This is a laboratory test and is not meant to be 
used at site. 


2 APPARATUS 


2.1 Tray —A square water tight tray ofinner dimensions 
450 mm x 450 mm x (25 to 50) mm (length x width 
x height) with a metal scale attached to the inside of the 
tray side. The graduations shall be clearly legible with 
an accuracy of 0.5 mm. 


2.2 Supports for the Brick — Two non-corrodible 
metal supports of half round or triangular cross-section 
of length 150 to 250 mm and of height 6 mm. The bars 
shall be so placed such that the broader side of the 
section rests on the tray. 


2.3 Weighing Balance — A weighing balance with an 
accuracy of 0.5 g. 


2.4 Hot Air Oven — A hot air oven capable of 
maintaining a temperature of 110+5 °C. 


2.5 Timing Device — Timing device such as stop 
watch or stop clock capable of indicating time nearest 
to ls. 


3 PROCEDURE 


3.1 Oven-dried Bricks 


Dry the bricks in the hot air oven at 110+5 °C for not 
less than 24 h so as to attain constant mass such that 
two consecutive masses taken at an interval of 2 h 
shall not vary by more than 0.20 percent. After drying 
cool the bricks in a room maintained at a temperature 
of 25+10 °C with relative humidity between 30 and 
70 percent such that the surface temperature is within 
3 °C of the ambient room temperature. 


3.2 Weigh the oven-dried cooled specimen to an 
accuracy of 0.5 g. Record the mass as M,. Measure the 
length and width of the specimen to the nearest 1 mm 
and calculate the surface area which will be in contact 
with the water. Determine the surface area of any other 
shape with similar accuracy. 


3.3 Place the tray on a levelled surface. Place the 
supports in the tray partially filled with water and on 


top of supports keep a saturated brick, such that the 
brick surface is submerged in water up to a level of 
3 mm. Add water to adjust the 3 mm level and note the 
height of water on the metal scale fixed inside the tray. 
Remove the saturated brick. Now the tray is ready to 
take the dry brick to perform the test. 


3.4 Keep the oven-dried brick in the tray and maintain 
the water level such that the brick surface is submerged 
to the extent of 3 mm. Note the time of immersion and 
the specimen should be in contact with the water for 
1 min. The dry brick will start sucking the water and 
hence water should be replenished continuously such 
that the specimen surface is under 3 mm water during 
the test. After 1 min lift the specimen from the water 
and wipe off the surface water with damp cloth. Weigh 
the partially wet specimen to the accuracy of 0.5 g, 
and record the mass as M,. Wiping shall be completed 
within 10 s after lifting the specimen from water and 
weighing shall be completed within 2 min. 
NOTE — Placing the bricks in the tray containing water 
shall be quick without splashing. Set the brick with rocking 
motion to avoid air entrapment. The specimen surface in 
contact with the water should be plain and the surface with 
frog or depression should face up avoiding the water contact. 
Calculate the net area for the cored or perforated specimen. 


3.5 Calculation and Report 


The difference in the masses of dry and partially wet 
specimen is the amount of water absorbed by the 
specimen during | minute contact with the water, 
designated as x (x = M, — M,). The x shall be converted 
to kg. The initial rate of water absorption (IRA) shall be 
calculated as follows: 


x 


Surface area (in m’) in contact with the water 
where 
IRA = Initial rate of absorption in kg/m?/min; and 
x= gain in mass, in kg. 
The surface area is the total surface area of the brick 


which is in contact with water. In case of bricks having 
frog, this shall also include the area of frog. 


Test a minimum of five specimens and report average 
IRA to an accuracy of 0.1 kg/m?/min. 


In case of the IRA values varying beyond 15 percent 
of the mean value, the same shall be discarded. In such 
cases, the average of minimum 4 values shall be reported.

Bureau of Indian Standards 


BIS is a statutory institution established under the Bureau of Indian Standards Act, 2016 to promote harmonious 
development of the activities of standardization, marking and quality certification of goods and attending to 
connected matters in the country. 


Copyright 


BIS has the copyright of all its publications. No part ofthese publications may be reproduced in any form without 
the prior permission in writing of BIS. This does not preclude the free use, in the course of implementing the 
standard, of necessary details, such as symbols and sizes, type or grade designations. Enquiries relating to 
copyright be addressed to the Director (Publications), BIS. 


Review of Indian Standards 


Amendments are issued to standards as the need arises on the basis of comments. Standards are also reviewed 
periodically; a standard along with amendments is reaffirmed when such review indicates that no changes are 
needed; if the review indicates that changes are needed, it is taken up for revision. Users of Indian Standards 
should ascertain that they are in possession of the latest amendments or edition by referring to the latest issue of 
“BIS Catalogue” and “Standards: Monthly Additions’. 


This Indian Standard has been developed from Doc No.: CED 30 (15751).
